content:
There are reports that code discovered in the camera app of the latest iOS 27 beta seems to foreshadow several major professional photography and video recording features coming soon.

Although the built-in camera app has gradually added more features over time, for an app primarily designed for casual point-and-shoot photography, these discoveries are still somewhat surprising…

Apple has always tried to strike a balance between the two — on one hand, designing its camera app to be extremely easy to operate for quick snapshots; on the other hand, providing a degree of creative control for users who want to use it as a serious camera. However, even though the app has gradually evolved, most photography and videography enthusiasts still tend to use third-party apps.

If these discoveries prove true, the introduction of some powerful features normally seen only on professional cameras could completely change the current landscape. Developer pdfu says he has found code supporting four major features, none of which have been enabled in any current beta version.

Exposure assist tools

Judging exposure by eye is often unreliable, especially when viewing the iPhone screen in harsh sunlight. Most professional cameras support a histogram function that accurately displays exposure status, while video editing software typically uses a waveform display as an alternative. Pdfu says he has found code related to these two features in the beta version.

Focus Peaking

How much of a scene — from the nearest foreground to the farthest background — remains sharp and in focus is affected by several factors, but in certain shooting situations, only part of the scene will be sharp. Likewise, judging by eye which areas are in focus and which are not is not entirely reliable, so professional-grade cameras have specially adopted a method called focus peaking.

When this feature is enabled, an overlay can be activated to highlight the areas in focus, usually in red — although the example on the left uses yellow.

Overexposure (highlight clipping) warning

The biggest risk from exposure errors is overexposure. Generally speaking, if shadows are underexposed, they can usually be rescued in post-processing — unless the situation is extremely severe, shadows rarely end up completely black (i.e., with RGB values at zero). Overexposure is far more serious, because highlights can easily end up completely "clipped" — that is, exceeding an RGB value of 255 — and no amount of post-processing can recover them.

Many professional cameras use what is called a zebra pattern indicator, marking fully clipped areas with red diagonal stripes. Some cameras also allow users to manually set the threshold for this warning, so that you can be alerted when approaching overexposure (e.g., 90%) rather than waiting until it actually clips to issue the warning.

This feature is also shown on the right side of the image above.

Manual focus

Currently, although the camera app can lock focus on a particular element in the frame, it must also lock the exposure of that point at the same time via AE/AF Lock (auto exposure / auto focus).

The report states that Apple has been testing a true manual focus function operated via a slider within the camera app. Pdfu says this feature may be limited to one or more upcoming new iPhone models.

Other features

In addition to the professional features, there are reportedly plans to add an option to capture a burst of timed selfies in succession. Often when people want to take group photos they want to take several shots; this feature would allow everyone to place the iPhone on a tripod or other flat surface, then snap a continuous series of photos, and choose the one everyone is happy with.

Finally, there are also indications that a new image processing method will be adopted to accommodate the variable aperture design expected to appear on the iPhone 18 Pro.

9to5Mac's take

All of the features mentioned above have not been enabled in any iOS 27 beta version to date. I myself would be surprised if Apple puts these features in the built-in camera app rather than restricting them to Final Cut Camera — but the report does seem fairly credible.

What do you think of this report? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
